---
title: "Command line"
---

This documents the command-line interface (CLI) and its Rust counterparts,
including some function signatures and explanation of the choices we've made.
This document is primarily to help us (the developers) stay focused on the
package's scope.

{{< include /docs/includes/_design-status.qmd >}}

## {{< var wip >}} `init` {#cli-init}

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do init [PATH] --verbose
```

This will create an empty `.zenodo.toml` file that contains all the metadata
fields available for a Zenodo deposit, but with no values filled in, excluding a
partially filled in `zendo_id` for the project. The file is by default stored in
the current directory (i.e., `.`) but can be specified as a relative or absolute
path. This simple command is helpful to get started with making a new Zenodo
deposit, as well as standardizing the name and structure of the file.

## {{< var wip >}} `list` {#cli-list}

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do list --sandbox
```

The `list` command fetches the stored Zenodo token and gets all Zenodo deposits
listed in the account connected to that token. Both the CLI and the internal
Rust interface are used in other functions like `publish()` to find whether a
deposit exists or not.

## {{< var wip >}} `get` {#cli-get}

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do get [METADATA_FILE] --sandbox
```

The `get` command will get the Zenodo deposit JSON based on the metadata file
provided. If the deposit doesn't exist, it will output a message about not
finding a match. This is useful for checking if a deposit already exists for a
given set of metadata, and if so, getting the deposit information to use for
updating or publishing it. Internally uses the Rust functions within `list()` to
get the list of deposits and uses that to find the deposit that matches the
content of the metadata file using the `zendo_id`.

## {{< var wip >}} `sync` {#cli-sync}

```bash {filename="Terminal"}
zen-do sync [METADATA_FILE] --to [FORMAT]
```

There are many different file formats and standards that contain similar or even
identical metadata, but that are structured slightly differently. The `sync`
command helps to keep one "source of truth" between these different formats for
those cases where a repository might need different formats for different
purposes. For example, GitHub will look for a `CITATION.cff` file to display the
citation information for a repository, but doesn't recognize other formats (like
`.zenodo.toml`). Rather than manually keeping these different files in sync, the
`sync` command can simplify this syncing task.

We decided to only sync from `.zenodo.toml` to other formats, rather than allow
any format to be synced to any other format because we want the `.zenodo.toml`
file to be the "single source of truth" for a project's metadata. This means
that any changes to the metadata must be done in the `.zenodo.toml` file and
`sync` can update the other formats. This also simplifies the implementation and
testing of the `sync` command, as we only need to implement the logic for
syncing from `.zenodo.toml` to other formats, rather than having to handle
syncing between all possible pairs of formats.

There are several different formats that we've encountered that would be useful
to keep synchronized with the `.zenodo.toml` file, including:

- {{< var planned >}} `.zenodo.json`: This is the file format that Zenodo looks
  for in their existing [GitHub release to record
  integration](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/github/describe-software/). Both the
  JSON and TOML formats are equivalent in content.
- {{< var planned >}} `CITATION.cff`: GitHub uses this file to [display the
  citation](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-citation-files)
  information for a repository when it is in the root of the repository. This
  contains only a subset of the metadata found in the `.zenodo.toml` file.
- {{< var planned >}} `pyproject.toml`: While this file is almost entirely used
  only for Python projects, it contains similar metadata fields to the
  `.zenodo.toml` file, such as the project name, description, authors, and
  license.
- {{< var planned >}} `codemeta.json`: This file is used to describe software
  metadata in a machine-readable format, following the
  [CodeMeta](https://codemeta.github.io/) standard. It contains similar metadata
  fields to the `.zenodo.toml` file.
- {{< var planned >}} `_quarto.yml`: This file is used to build
  [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) documents. Like `pyproject.toml`, it also
  contains similar metadata fields to the `.zenodo.toml` file, such as the
  title, description, and authors.
- {{< var planned >}} `DESCRIPTION`: This is a typical file found in R projects.
  It is necessary for developing and building R packages. As with
  `pyproject.toml`, it contains similar metadata fields to the `.zenodo.toml`
  file, such as the package name, description, authors, and license.

The `--to` argument takes a single format only, so `sync` must be used multiple
times to sync to multiple formats---one time for each format. This matches
similar "converter" packages, e.g. [pandoc](https://pandoc.org).

## {{< var planned >}} `update` {#cli-update}

```bash
zen-do update [METADATA-FILE] --sandbox --draft --yes
```

The `update` command takes a `.zenodo.toml` metadata file and updates the
contents with the Zenodo deposit, which also updates the record. It doesn't lead
to a new DOI, as it doesn't change the files in the deposit---only updated
metadata. This command is useful if you have a typo in one of the fields or
forgot to add some information, but you don't want to re-upload the same file
and create a new DOI.

`update` has one required argument, `[METADATA-FILE]` which is the path to the
`.zenodo.toml` file. By default, it looks for the file in the working directory.
The optional argument `--sandbox` tells the command to update a deposit in the
sandbox environment instead of updating it in Zenodo's main environment. The
second optional argument `--draft` updates the deposit without publishing to the
record, making it possible to check the deposit before publishing. Lastly,
`update` prompts for confirmation before actually updating, but with the `--yes`
flag, that confirmation is bypassed, which is useful for continuous delivery
workflows.

If no deposit exists then `update` will fail. A deposit needs to first be
published as a record (e.g., with `publish`) before any content can be updated.

## {{< var planned >}} `discard` {#cli-discard}

```bash
zen-do discard [METADATA-FILE] --sandbox
```

The `discard` command cancels a deposit that is in the "editable" state. This
happens when using the `--draft` argument in e.g. `update` or `publish`. This is
useful if you make a mistake with starting a deposit and want to cancel while
staying within the CLI. Like the other commands `--sandbox` will discard changes
in the editable state for deposits on the Zenodo sandbox.

## {{< var planned >}} `publish` {#cli-publish}

```bash
zen-do publish [METADATA-FILE] --file [FILE1,FILE2] --draft --sandbox --yes
```

The `publish` command takes a metadata file (`.zenodo.toml`) as well as some
files in `--file` and uploads them to Zenodo. If a deposit doesn't exist (based
on the presence of the `zendo_id`), a deposit will be created. If a deposit does
exist, the metadata will be overwritten by the metadata in the file, all files
will be deleted and the new files will be uploaded instead. If `--draft` is
used, the deposit doesn't get formally published as a new record, otherwise it
will immediately be created into a record with a corresponding DOI. If
`--sandbox` is used, the deposit and record will be created in the sandbox
environment on Zenodo. The `--yes` flag, like for the other commands, is used to
bypass the confirmation prompt.

Unlike the `update` command, this *requires* files to upload and will also
create a new version and thus a new DOI. If only the metadata needs to be
updated or fixed, use `update`, not `publish`.
